title: A model that scores too well, and a model that will not converge
prescribes: When metrics look too good, suspect leakage before celebrating: rank feature importances, test the suspect feature alone, and ask whether it could be known at prediction time. When training will not converge, check scaling before the architecture.
applied: Injected a plausible post-outcome column (`retention_call_logged`) into the churn frame, diagnosed it from the fitted coefficients, and separately reproduced a non-convergence bug by removing the scaler.
narrative: Adding one column takes test ROC-AUC from 0.8490 to 0.9830. A +0.1340 jump from a single feature on a problem this noisy is not a breakthrough, it is a symptom -- and the plausible-sounding name is exactly why it would survive review.

The diagnosis takes two steps. First, the standardised coefficients: `retention_call_logged` dominates at 2.35, roughly 2.6x the next feature. Second, the confirmation -- that column alone, with no other input, scores 0.9465 AUC. No legitimate customer attribute predicts churn that well.

The fix is not statistical, it is temporal: a retention call is logged *because* the account was flagged as churning, so the value does not exist at scoring time. It is dropped, and the model goes back to 0.8490 -- which is the number that will hold in production.

The second bug is more mundane and more common. With max_iter=50 and unscaled inputs (TotalCharges spans four orders of magnitude more than SeniorCitizen), lbfgs fails to converge and scores 0.7940; adding a StandardScaler under the same iteration cap gives 0.8415. The instinct to raise max_iter or blame the model would have wasted an afternoon.

takeaway: Both bugs were found by asking a question rather than tuning: could this value exist at prediction time, and is the optimiser actually converging?
